lessons.title: CSS is paint and clothes
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## HTML builds it, CSS styles it

HTML is like the walls of a house. **CSS** is the paint, the furniture and the decorations. CSS stands for *Cascading Style Sheets*.

CSS lives in its own file, `style.css`. The HTML page connects to it with a `<link>` tag in the `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
```

### A CSS rule

```css
h1 {
  color: purple;
}
```

- `h1` is the **selector**: *which* elements to style.
- `color` is the **property**: *what* to change.
- `purple` is the **value**: *how* to change it.
- Every line ends with a semicolon `;` and the rule sits inside curly braces `{ }`.

This rule makes **every** `<h1>` on the page purple.

### New words

- **CSS** (*Cascading Style Sheets*): the language that styles web pages.
- **Selector**: picks which elements a rule styles.
- **Property**: the thing you change, like `color` or `font-size`.
- **Value**: what you change it to, like `purple` or `24px`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Two rules: one paints the heading orange, the other makes paragraphs bigger. `px` means *pixels*, the tiny dots on your screen.

Volcanoes

Lava can be hotter than 1,000 °C.

lessons.title: Selectors, properties and values
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## CSS fundamentals

**CSS** (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation: color, type, spacing, layout. Keeping it in a separate file separates *structure* (HTML) from *presentation* (CSS), so one stylesheet can restyle a whole site.

### Anatomy of a rule

```css
/* comment */
h1 {                    /* selector */
  color: darkslateblue; /* declaration = property: value; */
  font-size: 2.5rem;
}
```

Several declarations make a **declaration block**. A missing `;` or `}` silently breaks the rules after it, so check those first when something doesn't apply.

### Values and units

| Kind | Examples | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Colors | `navy`, `#1d4ed8`, `rgb(29 78 216)` | Names are easy; hex and rgb are precise |
| Absolute length | `16px` | Fixed size |
| Relative to root font | `1.25rem` | Scales with the user's font-size setting, so prefer it for text |
| Relative to element font | `1.5em` | Compounds when nested |
| Percent | `50%` | Relative to the parent |

### Inheritance and the cascade

Some properties, like `color` and `font-family`, **inherit**: set them on `body` and every element below gets them. When two rules set the same property on the same element, the **cascade** decides: more specific selectors win, and among equals the later rule wins.

### New words

- **Declaration**: one `property: value;` pair.
- **Inherit**: when a child element takes a parent's value automatically.
- **rem** (*root em*): a length relative to the root (`<html>`) font size.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Styles set on `body` (font and color) are inherited by everything inside it. The `h1` rule then overrides the inherited color.

lessons.title: Classes, IDs and specificity
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Targeting elements precisely

| Selector | Matches | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Every element of that type | `p` |
| Class | Elements with `class="badge"` | `.badge` |
| ID | The one element with `id="featured"` | `#featured` |
| Descendant | `.highlight` anywhere inside `#intro` | `#intro .highlight` |
| Compound | Elements with **both** | `p.badge` |
| Group | Either selector | `h1, h2` |

An element can have several classes (`class="badge new"`). An ID must be unique on the page. Most teams style with classes and keep IDs for anchors and scripts.

### Specificity

When rules conflict, the more **specific** selector wins, regardless of order. Count it like a score of (IDs, classes, types):

| Selector | Score |
| --- | --- |
| `p` | (0, 0, 1) |
| `.highlight` | (0, 1, 0) |
| `#intro p` | (1, 0, 1) |
| `#intro .highlight` | (1, 1, 0) |

Compare left to right: one ID beats any number of classes. That's why `.highlight` loses to `#intro p` even though it's written later. Only when scores tie does the later rule win.

Avoid `!important` to force a win: it makes the next conflict harder to fix. Raise specificity just enough instead.

### New words

- **Specificity**: the weight that decides which conflicting rule applies.
- **Descendant selector**: two selectors separated by a space, matching elements nested inside others.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: The `#tips p` rule (one ID + one type) beats `.warning` (one class), so the warning paragraph stays gray. The last rule fixes it with `#tips .warning`, which scores higher.

lessons.title: Boxes inside boxes
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Every element is a box

To a browser, every element is a rectangle with layers, like a framed picture on a wall:

1. **Content**: the words or picture.
2. **Padding**: space *inside* the frame, around the content.
3. **Border**: the frame itself.
4. **Margin**: space *outside* the frame, between this box and its neighbors.

```css
.card {
  padding: 16px;          /* space inside */
  border: 3px solid black; /* the frame */
  margin: 24px;           /* space outside */
}
```

The border needs three things: thickness (`3px`), style (`solid`) and color (`black`).

> Tip: if text is squished against its border, add padding. If boxes bump into each other, add margin.

### New words

- **Padding**: space inside a box, around its content.
- **Border**: the line around a box.
- **Margin**: space outside a box.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Same content, two boxes. The second one has padding, a border and margin, so it's easier to read and doesn't touch its neighbors.

lessons.title: The box model
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## The box model

Every element generates a box with four areas, from the inside out: **content**, **padding**, **border**, **margin**.

### Shorthand

```css
padding: 20px;              /* all four sides */
padding: 10px 20px;         /* vertical | horizontal */
padding: 10px 20px 30px 40px; /* top | right | bottom | left (clockwise) */
border: 2px solid #334155;  /* width | style | color */
```

### How wide is a box?

By default (`box-sizing: content-box`), `width` sets only the **content** width. Padding and border are added on top:

> `width: 300px` + `padding: 20px` + `border: 2px` → **344px** on screen.

That surprises everyone. With `box-sizing: border-box`, `width` includes padding and border, so `width: 300px` means 300px on screen. Most teams set it everywhere:

```css
*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
```

### Margin collapse

When two block elements' vertical margins touch, they **collapse** into the larger of the two, not the sum. A 24px bottom margin above a 16px top margin gives a 24px gap. Padding and borders never collapse.

### Centering a block

A block with a set width can be centered with `margin: 0 auto;`: zero top/bottom, automatic (equal) left/right.

### New words

- **box-sizing**: whether `width` includes padding and border.
- **Margin collapse**: adjacent vertical margins merging into the larger one.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Both boxes have `width: 200px`, but the content-box one is wider on screen because its padding and border are added on top. The border-box one stays exactly 200px.

lessons.title: Lining things up with Flexbox
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Lining up toys on a shelf

Normally, boxes stack on top of each other like a tower. **Flexbox** lines them up in a row, like toys on a shelf.

You turn it on for the **parent** box (the shelf), and its children line up:

```css
.shelf {
  display: flex;
}
```

### Moving things around

- `justify-content: center;` moves the children to the middle, left to right.
- `align-items: center;` moves them to the middle, top to bottom.
- `gap: 16px;` puts space between the children.

Use both `center`s and you can put something right in the middle of a box. Lots of grown-up developers search the web for how to do that!

### New words

- **Flexbox**: a CSS tool for lining things up in a row (or a column).
- **Parent / children**: a box and the boxes directly inside it.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: The `.row` box is the parent. With `display: flex` its three children sit side by side, spread out by `gap`.

lessons.title: Flexbox
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Flexbox: one-dimensional layout

`display: flex` makes an element a **flex container** and its direct children **flex items**, laid out along a **main axis**.

### Container properties

| Property | Common values | Controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `flex-direction` | `row` (default), `column` | The main axis |
| `justify-content` | `flex-start`, `center`, `space-between`, `space-around` | Spacing **along** the main axis |
| `align-items` | `stretch` (default), `center`, `flex-start` | Alignment **across** the main axis |
| `gap` | `16px` | Space between items |
| `flex-wrap` | `nowrap` (default), `wrap` | Whether items move to a new line when out of room |

`justify-content` and `align-items` swap visual directions when `flex-direction` is `column`: they always follow the axes, not left/right.

### Item properties

`flex: 1` makes an item grow to share leftover space. `flex: 1 1 200px` means "start at 200px, grow and shrink as needed".

### When to use it

Flexbox shines for **one-dimensional** layouts: a nav bar, a row of buttons, centering, a row of cards that wraps. For two-dimensional layouts (rows *and* columns that line up), use Grid (next lesson).

### New words

- **Main axis / cross axis**: the direction items flow, and the one perpendicular to it.
- **Flex container / flex item**: the element with `display: flex`, and its direct children.

lessons.title: CSS Grid
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## CSS Grid: two-dimensional layout

Grid lays items out in rows **and** columns at once, so things line up both ways.

```css
.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
  gap: 16px;
}
```

### Defining tracks

| Value | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `200px 1fr` | A fixed 200px column, then one taking the rest |
| `repeat(3, 1fr)` | Three equal columns (same as `1fr 1fr 1fr`) |
| `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(150px, 1fr))` | As many ≥150px columns as fit: responsive without media queries |

The `fr` unit divides **free space** after fixed tracks and gaps are taken out.

### Placing and spanning items

Items fill cells in order by default. An item can span tracks:

```css
.hero { grid-column: span 2; }   /* two columns wide */
.tall { grid-row: span 2; }      /* two rows tall */
```

Or place it by **grid lines** (numbered from 1 at the start edge): `grid-column: 1 / 3` runs from line 1 to line 3, which is also two columns.

### Grid or Flexbox?

Use **Grid** when the layout is a 2D structure (page regions, galleries, dashboards). Use **Flexbox** when content flows in one direction (nav items, button groups). They nest happily: a grid cell can be a flex container.

### New words

- **Track**: a row or column of a grid.
- **Grid line**: the numbered boundaries between tracks.
- **Span**: how many tracks an item covers.

lessons.title: Responsive design
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Responsive design

A **responsive** page adapts to its viewport, from a 360px phone to a 2560px monitor. Most kids and teens browse primarily on phones, so many teams design **mobile-first**: write the small-screen layout as the default, then add media queries that enhance it for wider screens.

### 1. The viewport meta tag

Without it, phones pretend to be about 980px wide and shrink the page, so your media queries never fire:

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
```

### 2. Fluid sizing

- `max-width: 100%; height: auto;` on images keeps them inside their container.
- Prefer `%`, `fr`, `rem` and `minmax()` over fixed pixel widths.

### 3. Media queries

```css
/* mobile-first: one column by default */
.tracks { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; }

/* tablet and up */
@media (min-width: 700px) {
  .tracks { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); }
}
```

`min-width` queries (mobile-first) layer enhancements on; `max-width` queries (desktop-first) strip them away. Pick one direction per project for predictable cascades.

### Breakpoints

Choose breakpoints where **your content** breaks, not by device names. Shrink the window until the layout looks wrong; that width is a breakpoint.

### Testing

Use your browser's device toolbar (DevTools → toggle device mode) to try common widths, and test on a real phone before shipping.

### New words

- **Viewport**: the visible area of the page in the browser.
- **Breakpoint**: a width where the layout changes.
- **Mobile-first**: writing small-screen styles as the default and enhancing for larger screens.
